Definition: Frequency and severity of power outages experienced by businesses and households. Based on World Bank Enterprise Surveys, Afrobarometer, or national utility data. Reflects the quality of electricity supply beyond mere access — critical for running ICT equipment and data infrastructure.
Value Name: Severe (frequent daily outages or regular load shedding)
revision_notes: Cited 2020 World Bank report (itself drawing on older data) was fetched and confirms a picture of frequent daily outages and load shedding, consistent with the score. Cross-checked against the more recent World Bank Enterprise Surveys 2024 country profile for DRC (fetched and read): 77.4% of firms report experiencing electrical outages, with an average of 11.6 outages per typical month (above the low-income-country average of 10.1 and close to the Sub-Saharan Africa average of 13.4). At roughly one outage every 2-3 days, this sits at the severe end of the scale, above the 'weekly outages' (Poor) band and consistent with 'frequent...outages or regular load shedding' (Severe). Score of 1 (Severe) confirmed on fresher, primary evidence.
revised_comments: Grid reliability in the Democratic Republic of Congo remains severe, with businesses experiencing frequent power outages and regular load shedding. World Bank Enterprise Surveys (2024) find that 77.4% of firms report electrical outages, averaging 11.6 outages per month — above both the low-income-country average (10.1) and broadly in line with the Sub-Saharan Africa average (13.4). This level of disruption, occurring roughly every two to three days, reflects an aging and constrained national grid dominated by a single interconnected system, as documented by the World Bank's analysis of DRC's electricity access challenges.
